A chortle is a specific type of laugh — one that is joyful, gleeful, and a little triumphant. It is louder than a chuckle and more uncontrolled, but it is not a full roar of laughter. Think of it as a warm, bubbling laugh that bursts out of someone who is deeply amused and quite pleased — either with something they just heard, something they thought of, or something that went their way.
What makes a chortle different from other laughs?

There are many words for laughter in English, and each one captures a slightly different feeling. To understand a chortle precisely, it helps to compare it:

  • A giggle is light, high-pitched, and often a little shy or nervous.
  • A chuckle is quiet and inward — you chuckle to yourself, softly.
  • A snicker has a sly or mean edge — you snicker at someone, not with them.
  • A guffaw is a loud, booming burst of laughter — big and unrefined.
  • A chortle sits between a chuckle and a guffaw. It is warm and hearty, but not enormous. It has a kind of rumbling, snorting quality to it. Crucially, it carries a feeling of self-satisfied delight — the person chortling is not just amused, they feel a little smug or gleeful about it.
The emotional flavour of a chortle:

This is the most important thing to understand: a chortle is not just any happy laugh. It has a specific emotional texture — gleeful self-satisfaction. You might hear a chortle from:

  • Someone who just thought of a clever joke and is pleased with themselves for it.
  • A person who correctly predicted something and is now saying, "I knew it!"
  • Someone reading a funny book alone in a room, deeply entertained.
  • A child who has just pulled off a small mischief and finds it hilarious.

There is something almost private about a chortle — it often feels like the person is amused on their own terms, for their own reasons, regardless of whether anyone else finds it funny. It is warm and good-natured, not cruel, but it does carry a tiny whiff of smugness or triumph.
How it is used in sentences:

• "A chortle escaped him as he read the punchline." — The laugh came out involuntarily, bubbling up with delight.
  • "She let out a hearty chortle when she realised she had been right all along." — The triumphant, self-satisfied quality is on full display here.
  • "His chortle echoed through the quiet library, earning him a sharp look." — It was audible, unguarded, and a bit too loud for the setting.
  • "The old man's chortle was infectious — warm and rumbling." — It describes the physical quality: deep, rounded, slightly snorty.

"Chortle" is not a formal word. It belongs to casual, descriptive writing — fiction, storytelling, light journalism, or everyday speech. Writers use it when they want to convey not just that someone laughed, but how they laughed and what feeling drove that laugh. If a character chortles, you immediately know they are tickled and pleased, not just politely amused.
The full picture in one sentence:

A chortle is a warm, hearty, somewhat rumbling laugh that bubbles out of someone who is genuinely delighted and a little self-satisfied — louder than a chuckle, softer than a guffaw, and always carrying a note of gleeful triumph.
